subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — Medicine & Public Health Through Time
subtitle: How understanding of disease, medicine, and public health developed from ancient times to the present.

data.targetWord: an ancient Greek theory that the body contained four fluids — blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile — and that illness resulted from their imbalance; it influenced medicine for many centuries

examples.en-GB: A medieval physician might prescribe bloodletting to restore the balance of the four humours in a feverish patient.

data.targetWord: the belief that disease was caused by bad air from rotting waste or unpleasant smells — a common explanation from medieval times through the nineteenth century, now known to be incorrect

examples.en-GB: Miasma theory was wrong about the cause of cholera, but it still encouraged people to clean streets and remove waste.

data.targetWord: the scientific idea developed in the nineteenth century that many diseases are caused by microorganisms such as bacteria and viruses — it transformed medicine, surgery, and public health

examples.en-GB: Pasteur and Koch provided key evidence for germ theory, showing that specific microbes caused specific diseases.

data.targetWord: giving a weakened, dead, or harmless part of a disease-causing organism to help the body build immunity — it prevents disease before infection and is different from antibiotics which treat infection afterwards

examples.en-GB: Edward Jenner developed vaccination against smallpox in 1796 using cowpox material, creating a safer method than earlier inoculation.

data.targetWord: a medicine that kills or slows the growth of bacteria — antibiotics do not work against viruses and overuse can lead to antibiotic resistance

examples.en-GB: Penicillin, developed for mass use in the 1940s, was an antibiotic that transformed treatment of bacterial infections.

data.targetWord: a substance or method used to prevent infection by killing or reducing germs — Joseph Lister applied this to surgery in the 1860s using carbolic acid, greatly reducing post-operative deaths

examples.en-GB: Joseph Lister's use of carbolic acid as an antiseptic dramatically reduced infection rates in surgery.

data.targetWord: actions taken to improve the health of a whole population — including clean water, sewers, vaccination programmes, food safety, housing improvements, and government legislation

examples.en-GB: The 1875 Public Health Act was a major public health measure, requiring local councils to provide clean water and sewers.

data.targetWord: an ancient Greek physician linked to the idea that illness had natural causes and that doctors should observe patients carefully and look for natural rather than supernatural explanations

examples.en-GB: Hippocrates is often called the 'father of medicine' because he encouraged natural explanations and careful observation.

data.targetWord: a Greek doctor working in the Roman Empire whose ideas about anatomy and the four humours became extremely influential in European medicine for centuries, even though some were based on animal dissection and contained errors

examples.en-GB: Galen's ideas about the four humours were taught in medieval universities and remained dominant until the Renaissance.

data.targetWord: the medical tradition of the Islamic world from the 700s onward, which preserved, organised, and developed knowledge from Greek, Roman, Persian, and Indian traditions — scholars such as Ibn Sina and Al-Razi made major contributions

examples.en-GB: Islamic medical scholars translated Greek texts and added new knowledge, which was later translated into Latin and used in European universities.

data.targetWord: a Renaissance anatomist who used human dissection to produce detailed illustrations of the body in 1543, correcting some of Galen's errors and showing the importance of direct observation

examples.en-GB: Vesalius showed that some of Galen's anatomy was wrong because Galen had relied partly on animal dissections.

data.targetWord: an English physician who in 1628 explained the circulation of blood, showing that the heart acts as a pump and blood circulates around the body — improving understanding of physiology

examples.en-GB: William Harvey's explanation of blood circulation challenged older ideas and showed how observation could correct ancient theories.

data.targetWord: a nineteenth-century physician who investigated a cholera outbreak in Soho, London in 1854 by mapping deaths and linking them to a contaminated water pump — a landmark in using evidence to understand disease

examples.en-GB: John Snow's mapping of cholera deaths around the Broad Street pump showed that cholera spread through contaminated water.

data.targetWord: a nineteenth-century reformer whose 1842 report argued that poor sanitation caused disease and that improving drainage and water supplies would save lives — he believed in miasma theory but his practical solutions still improved public health

examples.en-GB: Chadwick's report was influential even though his miasma theory was wrong, because cleaning water supplies reduced waterborne disease.

data.targetWord: a French scientist who developed key evidence for germ theory in the 1860s, showing that microbes caused fermentation and decay and supporting the idea that microorganisms cause disease

examples.en-GB: Pasteur's work on germ theory helped Joseph Lister understand how to reduce infection in surgery.

data.targetWord: a German doctor who identified specific bacteria causing specific diseases including tuberculosis and cholera, strengthening germ theory through laboratory methods

examples.en-GB: Robert Koch's identification of specific bacteria made germ theory much more precise and scientifically convincing.

data.targetWord: a British law that made local councils responsible for clean water, sewers, rubbish collection, and public health officers — more effective than the earlier 1848 Act because it was compulsory

examples.en-GB: The 1875 Public Health Act was a turning point because it made sanitation a legal responsibility of local government, not just a voluntary option.

data.targetWord: the National Health Service, created in Britain in 1948 to provide healthcare funded through taxation and free at the point of use, improving access for people regardless of their ability to pay

examples.en-GB: Before the NHS, access to healthcare often depended on money or insurance; from 1948, it was available free at the point of use.

data.targetWord: a British scientist who in 1928 noticed that a mould called Penicillium killed bacteria in a laboratory dish — his discovery was later developed by Florey and Chain into penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic

examples.en-GB: Fleming's observation in 1928 was the starting point for penicillin, though it needed other scientists and wartime funding to become widely available.

data.targetWord: separating people, ships, or goods to prevent the spread of disease — used in medieval port cities and during plague outbreaks as a practical response to contagion, even before germ theory

examples.en-GB: Medieval port cities used quarantine to hold ships and passengers before allowing them entry, hoping to prevent plague spreading.

data.targetWord: the event in London in 1858 when hot weather made the polluted River Thames smell terrible near Parliament, creating political pressure that helped push through the building of Joseph Bazalgette's modern sewer system

examples.en-GB: The Great Stink of 1858 showed how political pressure, public discomfort, and engineering could combine to drive public health reform.

data.targetWord: a person in medieval and early modern times who performed basic surgery, tooth pulling, bloodletting, and similar procedures — distinct from physicians who gave medical advice

examples.en-GB: A barber-surgeon might perform bloodletting to restore humour balance, while a physician gave advice about diet and lifestyle.

data.targetWord: a major pandemic that reached England in 1348-1349, killing a large proportion of the population — it exposed the limits of medieval medicine and encouraged some public health measures such as street cleaning

examples.en-GB: The Black Death of 1348-1349 killed perhaps a third of England's population and showed how powerless medieval medicine was against epidemic disease.

data.targetWord: the study of the structure of the body through dissection and observation — Renaissance scholars such as Vesalius improved anatomy by studying human bodies directly rather than relying on ancient texts

examples.en-GB: Renaissance anatomy improved understanding of the body's structure but did not immediately lead to better treatments for infection or pain.

data.targetWord: the development of bacteria that are no longer killed by a particular antibiotic, caused by overuse or misuse — a major modern public health challenge

examples.en-GB: Antibiotic resistance is a major modern public health challenge because overuse of antibiotics allows bacteria to evolve and become resistant.

data.targetWord: a disease spread through contaminated water that caused severe diarrhoea and dehydration — cholera outbreaks in nineteenth-century Britain drove major public health reforms including clean water supplies and sewers

examples.en-GB: Cholera outbreaks in the 1840s and 1850s helped convince the government to invest in clean water and sewers in industrial cities.

data.title: Key developments in medicine in approximate chronological order
items: Hippocrates promotes natural explanations for illness (ancient Greece)
Galen's humoural ideas influence European medicine for centuries
Islamic scholars preserve and develop medical knowledge (700s-1200s)
Vesalius improves anatomy through human dissection (1543)
Jenner develops smallpox vaccination (1796)
Pasteur and Koch develop germ theory (1860s-1880s)
Lister introduces antiseptic surgery (1860s)
Fleming discovers penicillin (1928)
NHS created in Britain (1948)

data.title: Cause-consequence chain: public health reform in nineteenth-century Britain
items: Industrial cities grow rapidly with overcrowded housing and polluted water
Cholera outbreaks cause high death rates in poor urban areas
Reformers like Chadwick publish reports linking poor sanitation to disease
Public fear and political pressure build for government action
Parliament passes the 1848 Public Health Act (limited)
The Great Stink of 1858 creates urgent political pressure in London
The 1875 Public Health Act makes councils legally responsible for sanitation

data.title: Steps from Fleming's discovery to penicillin saving lives
items: Fleming notices Penicillium mould killing bacteria in his lab (1928)
Florey and Chain develop methods to purify and test penicillin (1930s-1940s)
Government and pharmaceutical companies fund mass production during World War Two
Penicillin becomes widely available and saves lives from bacterial infections
